title: delivered_amount, faucet funding and Testnet endpoint history
abstract: Operational lessons on faucet wallets, partial payments, validated settlement and historical transaction availability.
tags: faucet funding and Testnet endpoint history
body:
For XRP Payment settlement, delivered_amount is evidence of what the destination actually received. Checking the requested Amount alone can accept an underpayment when partial-payment semantics apply. Our checks bind destination, currency, amount and invoice identity to the intended purchase. Escrow settlement has its own validation and object checks. Issued-token escrow additionally requires the exact RippleState balance delta, with the correct currency, issuer and sign. A requested amount is never sufficient proof of delivery.

Faucet funding supplies test assets for experiments and is separate from settling a purchase. A faucet balance is not revenue or evidence of customer adoption. The payment receipt should identify the network and exact asset, and distinguish a simulated transaction from a validated Testnet transaction. Testnet balances have no redeemable value.

When a public server cannot find an older transaction, retain its hash and check an appropriate history endpoint. Missing history is an availability problem, not proof of failed settlement. A reader should see whether verification succeeded, failed or remains unresolved. Do not replace a missing result with a fresh payment simply to produce a successful receipt.

Author interpretation: reconcile each purchase using its exact asset, intended recipient and validated outcome. Keep setup funding out of purchase totals and preserve transaction evidence for independent verification. These boundaries make it possible to inspect a demonstration without confusing Testnet activity with real-world commercial settlement.
